cards.front: What are the four Claude product features named in Associate task 3.1?
cards.back: **Chat, Projects, Research and Artifacts.**

cards.front: When is plain chat the right choice?
cards.back: One-off questions, quick drafts or short brainstorms that need no reusable setup.

cards.front: What is a Claude Project?
cards.back: A self-contained workspace with its **own chats, knowledge base (uploaded files) and instructions**, for recurring work on the same material.

cards.front: Cue words that point to a Project?
cards.back: "Every week", "same documents", "same tone across chats", "recurring client work".

cards.front: What does Research do?
cards.back: Runs **several searches that build on each other**, explores different angles, and returns a thorough answer **with citations**, usually in minutes.

cards.front: Research requirements and costs?
cards.back: Paid plan, web search turned on; can also search connected Google Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, Docs). It **uses usage limits faster** than ordinary chat.

cards.front: Research gave citations. Can you skip checking?
cards.back: No. Citations make checking **easier**, but you still verify the claims that matter before sharing.

cards.front: What is an Artifact?
cards.back: A **standalone output** (document, deck, design, code, interactive tool) that opens beside the chat for editing, reuse and sharing.

cards.front: When does Claude tend to create an artifact?
cards.back: When content is significant and self-contained, something you'll likely edit or reuse outside the chat.

cards.front: What are Skills (in claude.ai)?
cards.back: Packaged instructions and resources that Claude loads **only when relevant** to a task.

cards.front: The team needs the final output as a real .docx or .xlsx. Which capability?
cards.back: **File creation** (code execution): Claude can create and edit Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files.

cards.front: Name the three model tiers in the Associate guide, lightest to most capable.
cards.back: **Haiku → Sonnet → Opus.**

cards.front: Haiku is best for...?
cards.back: Fast, low-cost, **high-volume, simple, well-defined** tasks: tagging, short replies, extracting fields, quick summaries.

cards.front: Sonnet is best for...?
cards.back: A **balance of speed and intelligence**: a strong default for everyday drafting, analysis and content work.

cards.front: Opus is best for...?
cards.back: **Complex reasoning**, nuanced analysis and long multi-step work where quality matters more than speed or cost. Slower and costlier.

cards.front: Is Opus always the top tier?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Lineups change; at the time of writing the docs list a higher tier (Claude Fable 5.1). Learn the trade-off, not names.

cards.front: Can a newer Sonnet beat an older Opus?
cards.back: Yes. Tier names show relative position within one generation, not a permanent ranking.

cards.front: On a subscription plan, does model choice still matter for cost?
cards.back: Yes. More capable models **use up usage limits faster**, even if you don't pay per message.

cards.front: The three dials of model selection?
cards.back: **Quality** needed, **speed** needed, **cost/volume**.

cards.front: Core rule for model fit?
cards.back: Use the **lightest model that reliably meets the quality bar**; move up only if it falls short.

cards.front: Efficiency-first vs capability-first?
cards.back: Efficiency-first: start light, test, upgrade if needed (high-volume, simple work). Capability-first: start strong on complex work, then optimize down. Both: **test on real examples**.

cards.front: Why is "always use the most capable model" wrong?
cards.back: It wastes cost and time on simple work and drains usage limits; it ignores the trade-off.

cards.front: Results from a light model are weak. What do you try before switching models?
cards.back: A clearer prompt, better context (Project files), task decomposition, or a higher effort level. Then move up a tier if needed.

cards.front: What is a multi-model workflow?
cards.back: A light model does bulk steps (sort, extract, draft) and a strong model does the judgment step, with human review where stakes demand it.

cards.front: Model quality disappoints. Is switching AI platforms the fix?
cards.back: Usually not. Choose a better-fit Claude model or improve the prompt; switching platforms doesn't address the trade-off.

cards.front: What is the context window?
cards.back: The amount of text Claude can consider at once in a chat (messages, replies, files, instructions): its **working memory**. Large but finite.

cards.front: Does a bigger context window mean perfect recall?
cards.back: No. In very long contexts earlier details get less attention ("context rot"). Curate and restart.

cards.front: Three moves for managing context?
cards.back: **Restart**, **summarize** (and carry forward), **persist** (Projects, memory, saved outputs).

cards.front: When should you restart a chat?
cards.back: New topic, drift, Claude repeating old mistakes, or nearing your usage limit in a long thread.

cards.front: What belongs in a good handoff summary?
cards.back: Goal and audience, decisions and reasons, key facts **with exact numbers and names**, open questions and next steps. Check it before reusing.

cards.front: What happens automatically when a long chat nears the limit (code execution on)?
cards.back: Claude **summarizes earlier messages** to keep going; full history is preserved, but long chats use more of your limit and summaries can lose precise details.

cards.front: What do Projects do when knowledge nears the context limit on paid plans?
cards.back: Switch to **retrieval (RAG)**: Claude searches the knowledge for relevant passages instead of reading all of it at once.

cards.front: How does Claude memory handle Projects?
cards.back: **Each Project has its own separate memory space**, so context stays separate between Projects.

cards.front: Pause memory vs reset memory?
cards.back: Pause: keeps existing memories, creates no new ones. Reset: **permanently deletes** all memories.

cards.front: What is an incognito chat?
cards.back: A chat that is not saved to chat history or memory. Useful for sensitive one-offs, but it **doesn't replace** organizational data policy.

cards.front: Who controls memory availability on Team/Enterprise plans?
cards.back: The **organization owner**; it is off for members by default until enabled and opted into.

cards.front: You paste the same style guide into every new chat. Better approach?
cards.back: Put it in a **Project's knowledge** and write Project instructions, so every chat there starts with it.

cards.front: Claude in a 2-day chat now quotes an outdated figure. Best fix?
cards.back: Ask for a summary of current decisions with correct figures, check it, and **start a fresh chat** (ideally in a Project holding the source file).
